utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, if you are ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. And I think we -- the Scheduling Order said that you have one hour for --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rebuttal evidence, argument, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence and General Mladic reiterate that General Mladic never intended nor ordered any crimes and acted honourably at all times to defend his people and his country amidst a time of conflict. We emphasise that our thoughts go out to all those aggrieved. It is in this light, Your Honours, we would like to start by responding to the Prosecution's use of the testimony given by RM070. The Prosecution has not provided evidence during their submission demonstrating that General Mladic knew about these wrong-doings or that they were reported to him. The Defence points out that it has been proven that where General Mladic had knowledge of crimes by others, he always issued orders seeking to have perpetrators disarmed, arrested, investigated, and prosecuted. One striking example addressed in both the submission of the Prosecution and the Defence was in relation to the Arkan's Tigers in Sanski Most and the order to remove paramilitaries. There is no indication that General Mladic would act differently in relation to these wrong-doings. The Defence notes that the Prosecution cannot rely on RM070's opinion testimony as being indicative of genocidal intent. RM070 themselves highlights not all Serbs are the same. At transcript page 17652, the witness quotes: "Because if there were -- there hadn't been for some Serb, she wouldn't be sitting here today. Because there are some good people among the Serbs." At transcript page 20805, the Prosecution invites the Chamber to consider the six strategic objectives as indications of a common plan encompassing genocidal intent. The Defence would like to stress that our position is the same as that of the Stakic, Krajisnik, and Sikirica Chambers, which found no evidence this specific general political doctrine carried any genocidal intent. Furthermore, Your Honours, the Prosecution's own expert, Robert Donia, acknowledged that General Mladic issued harsh warnings and expressed concern in relation to the creation of the six strategic objectives. At this stage, the Defence would like to express its awareness of the Chamber's perception communicated on 19 July 2012 that there "might not be a factual basis for the basis of the knowledge of the intent" of Mladic. I would now like to turn briefly to P431, the 16th Assembly transcript. At page 33 in e-court, page 37 of the hard copy, General Mladic is quoted as saying: "I would like to make one suggestion here that we adopt such a wisdom that we are against the war but that we will fight if attacked, and we do not want a war against the Muslims as a people, or against the Croats as a people, but against those who steered and pitted these peoples against us." Further, at page 35 in e-court, page 39 in hard copy, General Mladic is quoted as saying: "But that does not mean the Muslims have to be expelled or drowned. The minister would, it's a pity that we did not record it yesterday. To keep a long story short, as I said, they all gathered at my place, had a drink there, those from my village and from the neighbouring village, both Serbs and Muslims, all must take care of one another." These fragments fly in the face of genocidal intent. Further, at transcript page 20813, the Prosecution itself refers to P431, page 49, which the Defence has discovered is in error as the text can be found at page 37 in the hard copy, page 33 in e-court, and appears just before the text -- the first text that I just read, and the Prosecution implies that shifting the people from here to there is an organised campaign of ethnic cleansing, which is an interpretation completely out of context and irreconcilable with these remaining words which we have now drawn the Chamber's attention to. Yesterday the Prosecution submitted other personal statements and utterances of the accused as proof supporting counts in the indictment. We would recall the principle in dubio pro reo which is applied to these and also urge the Chamber to consider that these have been taken out of context as well by the Prosecution. Additionally, Your Honours, the Prosecution improperly made reference to events in 1991 and events relating to Croatia to attempt to establish the intent of General Mladic and to allege the commission of crimes attributable to him. This is at transcript pages 20807 through 20808. The Defence reiterates that such time-period and subject matter is beyond the scope of the indictment and has been repeatedly objected to by the Defence. If the Prosecution has not been able to establish criminal liability for the events occurring during the indictment, it is not permissible for it to expand the indictment period to include 1991 and Croatia, without going through the steps necessary to give appropriate notice to the accused and to seek to amend the indictment. At the outset of their response, the Prosecution, at 20803 of the transcript, referred to police figures being members of the JCE. Your Honours, I remind you of those arguments advanced by the Defence on Monday relying upon the Prosecution expert, Mr. Theunens, and the Prosecution's evidence demonstrating that police were not subordinated to General Mladic and that he exerted all possibilities within his authority to apprise the police minister and Karadzic about the actions of the police and paramilitary units operating within the auspices of the police. This is again P3095, P5133, and P5065, among others. Moving along, Your Honours, at transcript page 20817 and 20818, the Prosecution raised the notion that destruction of non-Serb cultural sites constituted evidence of genocidal intent and a genocidal campaign. The Prosecution, however, did not include this in the indictment for genocide. If the Prosecution tries to indicate that the Chamber ought to infer genocidal intent from the circumstances surrounding the alleged JCE, they surely cannot rely on unscheduled incidents of destruction. Your Honours, the Defence has with great detail outlined the evidence as to religious sites and their alleged destruction, and, similarly, our concerns about the quality of the same, which we regard as incapable of belief. I will not say any more about this, except to point out that the Prosecution did not offer any new or more detailed evidence on this topic to bolster the paucity of evidence that we brought to the attention of Your Honours during our submission on Monday. Further, at transcript page 20803, the Prosecution boldly asserts that the taking of UN personnel, which the Defence did not raise in our 98 bis submissions, is indicative of the common purpose behind the JCE constituting genocidal intent. Additionally, the taking of hostages is not properly pled in Counts 1 and 2 of the indictment. As both the Prosecution and Defence have raised in our 98 bis submissions, it is well established case law before the Tribunal to apply JCE to specific-intent crimes. However, in light of the lack of specificity in this indictment, this could have far-reaching and undesirable consequences to fairness to the accused and the development of future jurisprudence. In the briefest way, the Defence will now address the discussion of Directives 7 and 7.1 by the Prosecution which can be found at transcript page 20835. The assertion was made that Directive 7.1 adopted the entirety of Directive 7. This is contrary to the plain meaning of the language contained in Directive 7.1 which was issued by General Mladic. Indeed, looking at P1470, page 2 in English, just above the tasking of the VRS, the only part of Directive 7 which is taken over is identified as additional details on the intentions and possibilities of enemy forces which are said to be contained in Directive 7 and daily intelligence reports of the Main Staff. For the tasking of the VRS in Directive 7.1, it is said merely: "On the basis of Directive 7.1," and then the text proceeds to detail the tasking without reference to any of the controversial provisions of making life unbearable for civilians that are contained in Directive 7. Therefore, Your Honours, the Prosecution argument as to this directive is factually misplaced. P1465, the Krivaja 95 plan, does not contain the language from Directive 7 directing to make life unbearable for civilians, and in fact, the text of the same contains no illegal orders. P1084, cited by the Prosecution, is merely a map that General Mladic signed after the completion of Krivaja 95 and the map also does not contain any illegal orders to attack civilians. There thus is not available under this evidence any suggestion that the Krivaja operation and Directive 7.1 advocated any criminal intent or purpose. The position of the Prosecution taken yesterday as to the Krivaja operation is contradictory to their opening statements at transcript page 486 and the conclusions of their own military excerpt, Richard Butler. Your Honours, I will move on to some other outstanding points. In relation to our arguments about the liability of third party actors, the Prosecution at transcript page 20824 and onwards focussed primarily on Prijedor and largely failed to provide counter-arguments or citations to evidence on the record for the remaining municipalities and locations that were the subject of our original submission. The Prosecution spent considerable time on the command and control of General Mladic as to JNA infrastructure and equipment that became the VRS. The Defence, for purposes of Rule 98 bis, did not raise command and control over the VRS as an issue for a no case to answer submission. Rather, we were very succinct and clear that the arguments as to command and effective control that we were raising related to non-VRS actors, including the police, paramilitaries, Arkan's Tigers, and Skorpions. Thus, the Prosecution's arguments are misconceived and do not rebut our submissions on this topic. The Prosecution did briefly address the Skorpions but misapprehended the Defence submission. At this time, I would ask that we go into private session so I may discuss the testimony of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, could you at any point in time further briefly elaborate on what it is in the position of the Prosecution taken yesterday that is contradicting what is found in transcript page 486, that's the opening statement. If you could do so, not necessarily immediately but to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I could do so immediately. It might be easiest. In the opening statement, Your Honour, the Prosecution indicated that the military operation directed against the 28th division in Srebrenica enclave to stop the raids of the Armija BiH was not an illegitimate military action, saying it was a legitimate military action. Their inference yesterday that the Krivaja plan for that operation demonstrated criminal intent is therefore, in the position of the Defence, contradictory to their concession in opening statements that the military operation was not illegitimate. And that is the submission that I intended with that terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read on page 486 what the objective was but then the Prosecution added that Krivaja 95 had another objective, that was anything but legitimate. So, therefore, I'm -- I'm trying to understand exactly where -- how this contradicts where the Prosecution has stated that it was not only a military action but it was to attack Muslim civilian and UN observation posts or OPs in order to drive the Muslim population of the enclave into the small urban area of the enclave and create a humanitarian disaster. I'm just wondering whether this, I would say, this twofold objective is contradicted by what was said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is contradicted by what is contained in the Krivaja 95 order which I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are pointing at the contradiction between what the Prosecution said on page 486 compared to what they said yesterday. That is what I'm trying to understand reading page 486 and having listened to what the Prosecution said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was my recollection that they had said that the operation itself was not illegitimate and what happened later that they claimed it was part of the second -- additional objective, I guess they called it, was illegitimate. And my point is that the additional objective is not to be found in the text of the Directive 7.1 by General Mladic or the Krivaja 95 attack order, or the map as signed by General Mladic after the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your objection is mainly that the position taken by the Prosecution is not supported by evidence, which is, of course, not the same as a contradiction between what they said in the opening statement and what they said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You have said it much more succinctly than I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nothing in the Prosecution's submissions has rebutted the Defence submissions as to the Scorpions. The Prosecution, at transcript page 20853, has raised Kravica warehouse and has given a description of events at that location that are not supported by the evidence on the record. Rather, the Chamber should look to the evidence of RM374, a protected witness, who testified that there was a bus taking Muslims to Kravica warehouse, guarded by policemen on the bus. The Muslims on the bus overpowered the policemen and started exchanging fire from within the bus and with other policemen outside the bus. This is how one policeman was killed and another injured. This is at transcript page 12755 through 12779.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Madam Registrar. At transcript page 20850 to 20851, the Prosecution has challenged only the qualification of Kingori as a principal witness for the genocide in Srebrenica [sic]. While demonstrating their position that he is merely very important for their case, the Prosecution fails at all to address the conflicts between his testimony and several UNPROFOR officers that we believe renders Kingori's testimony incapable of brief. In relation to Skrljevita, at transcript page 20831 and onwards, the Prosecution asserts that the evidence demonstrated VRS officers intervened to have the perpetrators of the crime released from custody. The evidence cited does not support this proposition. P2371 is dated 10 September 1993 and is written on letterhead of the SDS Municipal Board of Sanski Most, not on behalf of any unit or formation of the VRS. This is a letter that is signed by the president of the SDS Municipal Board of Sanski Most and also by a captain who is a battalion commander in the VRS. Given the letterhead, it is clear that this is given in a personal capacity and is not an official VRS document. Further, the content of the letter amounts only to character reference and mitigating facts; whereas, the letter seeks the military court to "take this into account and pass fair judgement on him." The Prosecution's case has collapsed. They can try to now expand the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say "pass fear" or "pass fair"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Pass fair judgement, Your Honours. Fair, f-a-i-r.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, f-a-i-r. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution's case has collapsed. They can try to now expand the scope of the indictment to try and demonstrate intent and they can try to expand to have hostage-taking and destruction of religious sites bolster their case for concerted action between alleged JCE members. However, they have failed to explain how there can be concerted action between alleged JCE members, given the clear evidence on record of irreconcilable differences between General Mladic and SDS members like Karadzic, including the evidence that President Karadzic tried to remove General Mladic from his position and issued orders directly to VRS units bypassing General Mladic. The Defence recalls Exhibit P501 where General Mladic is trying to find out who has instructed the Sarajevo Corps to use aerial bombs against Sarajevo which the Main Staff did not order. Further the Prosecution has failed to demonstrate how there can be a meeting of the minds when Karadzic and Mladic differed and clashed as to their views on the use of Arkan and other paramilitary groups. In short, the Prosecution theory of the case only works if one ignores half of the evidence, and this Chamber must take the evidence as a whole. In our Monday submission, the Defence briefly addressed Exhibits P1547, P2141, P2142, D410, and P816 which dealt with prisoner exchanges and conditions. The Prosecution has not presented evidence contrary to this. The Defence implores the Chamber to acknowledge that exceptions to the count-based approach are essential to uphold the object and purpose of Rule 98 bis. Having a presumption against acquitting the accused of individual charges within a count is one thing, but to remove any opportunity for this to occur goes beyond what is necessary to prevent the danger of a piece-meal application of Rule 98 bis. A blanket approach by the Chamber offends the fundamental aspect of the Rule's purpose: To give effect to ensure the accused is tried expeditiously and to uphold the requirements of due process, and allows the Prosecution to exploit the count-based approach to disguise the evidentiary defects in their individual allegations. To adjudge and declare that the count-based approach should be applied to the present cases in accordance with the jurisprudence is to confirm that 98 bis is nothing more than a paper tiger, devoid of any practical application for the Defence by virtue of the fact that Trial Chambers apply an overly restrictive interpretation of it. Before this Tribunal, the Tadic Appeals Chamber stipulated that it is only appropriate to apply the notion of "common purpose" in relation to a joint criminal enterprise where the accused shared the intention to take part in a JCE and to further the criminal purpose of this enterprise. In addition, the accused must foresee the possible commission by other members of the group of offences that do not constitute the object of the common criminal purpose; paragraph 220 of the Tadic appeals judgement. Your Honours, the standard of Rule 98 bis is to determine if the Defence has a case to answer. At transcript page 20812, the Prosecution claims a "brutally efficient genocidal campaign" occurred. No evidence has been presented to substantiate a general factual finding of genocide. Their own expert, Ewa Tabeau, presented evidence that emphasised there were only small differences in losses among the three warring ethnic groups. We strongly believe that there is no case to answer as to Counts 1 and 2 because the Prosecution has failed to demonstrate why -- has failed to demonstrate by evidence capable of belief that General Mladic wilfully entered the JCE with a common purpose with foreseeability that others may resort to genocide to further that purpose. Lastly, we would invite the Chamber to consider the far-reaching consequences of including this many actors as sharing in the JCE's common purpose in light of the lack of specificity in the indictment. And with that, Your Honours, I again thank you on behalf of my client and my entire team for listening to our submissions. We have now completed our portion of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Judge Moloto has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, thank you so much. In light of the Defence's objection to the Prosecution referring to a period prior to the 12th of May, 1992, how does the Defence submit that Trial Chamber should interpret paragraph 5 of the fourth amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can get access to the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can read it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could, Your Honours. That would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 says: "Ratko Mladic committed each of the charged crimes in concert with others through his participation in several related joint criminal enterprises, each of which is described below. Radovan Karadzic and as of 12th May 1992, Ratko Mladic, were key members of an overarching joint criminal enterprise which lasted from at least October 1991 until November 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would ask the Chamber to interpret the indictment as it is supposed to be interpreted based upon the notice jurisprudence. Here, in paragraph 5, the participation of General Mladic is alleged to begin. His entry into the JCE is alleged to begin 12 May 1992. The schedule of the indictment giving incidents for which it is alleged that General Mladic has criminal responsibility have likewise focussed on the time-period post-12 May 1992. We have cited to jurisprudence relating to a JCE that indicates that the notice of a JCE needs to be specific as to the precise events alleged to be part of the JCE, the precise identity of perpetrators of the same, the precise manner of the accused's participation in the same, and we would argue that given that the indictment, this indictment, claims to limit General Mladic's criminal liability as flowing from 12 May 1992 onwards that this evidence that predates that time-period which has not been put in the indictment should not be considered for purposes of the guilt or innocence of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I understand you. The Defence objects to the Prosecution referring to actions of Mr. Mladic prior to the 12th of May, but the Defence does not object to the Prosecution talking about events by other participants which constitute JCE which were committed before 12th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's -- I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I have two questions for you: The first one is that you referred to P501, where you said General Mladic is trying to find out who has instructed the Sarajevo Corps to use aerial bombings against Sarajevo which the Main Staff did not order. Could you be a bit more precise where that exactly is found in P501.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can pull it up, Your Honours, and I might be able to. My recollection was that the document reads: We have information that you are planning on using an aerial bomb against Sarajevo. Please advise us. Please advise us - don't have the document here - how that has been issued since the Main Staff is supposed to be issuing them. If the Supreme Command has issued an order directly, it should be sent to the Main Staff. That's my recollection of the document. I hope I have the right one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perhaps what I wanted to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I can -- since we are done at the break, I can find that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can do that during the break. I'm looking forward to your answer. Then, I have one other question, which is the following: You very much insisted on General Mladic never have given any inappropriate order. You -- you certainly will remember that the Chamber has listened to an intercepted telephone conversation in which the issue of engaging Pofalici where not many Serbs were living was dealt with. Could you explain to us -- Mr. Mladic would like to be consulted, but let me first finish my question without being interrupted. Could you further elaborate on how this Chamber would have to interpret and have to look at such a telephone conversation and this observation about to engage Pofalici where not many Serbs are living. If you want to consult before you answer the question with Mr. Mladic, then, of course, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate the opportunity to consult and then I will attempt to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after consulting with my colleague and the General, and recalling that particular purported intercept, we remind the Chamber first and foremost that we have objected to the authenticity of many of the intercepts and I believe that intercept as well. But to look at the content of the same, there is another meaning behind the same. Where the VRS attacks enemy formations in a particular location, if there are Serbs that lived nearby, there's always the potential for reprisals against those Serbs by the ABiH forces. And so the intercept, if authentic, has an alternative meaning behind it that is equally reasonable under the evidence and in the principle of in dubio pro reo, the inferences must go towards the innocence of the accused. There is this meaning of limiting the ability of the enemy to undertake reprisals aimed against your own friendly civilians who may be in the area. And that would be the -- what I have to attempt to answer Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would have one follow-up question or perhaps rather to -- to see whether we agree on a matter, which is that in this telephone conversation, if it is reliable, if it is authentic that nothing is said about any military target in Pofalici but rather is talking about firing at Pofalici. And if we missed something that there was any specific military target mentioned elsewhere so that we could understand this to be an indication of to engage that military target at Pofalici, I'd like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My recollection, Your Honours, during the testimony when this was brought up was that there was a discussion of when artillery plans are made within the army that specific locations are identified on a map and that when communications are given it -- the common term is used rather than the precise location that would be known to those looking at the map together. That's all that I recall as being in the evidence upon this. We have, of course, intend to present more during our Defence case in-chief but that is irrelevant now for 98 bis. But that's all that I recall as being in evidence. Your Honour is correct that the purported intercept itself does not give any more specific detail, apart from just saying Pofalici, as to the intended target of the action. But there was, I believe, some evidence of maps having pre-coded targets included on them, such that commanders could refer using general terms and those on the other end looking at the same map would know which target is -- is intended. But I do concede that the intercepted itself as recorded again does not have any further specification, apart from saying just Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as far as other materials is concerned, is there in the evidence to be found anything which specifically, in maps or whatever way, specifically refers to Pofalici as being the location of any military target? I don't expect an answer right from the top of your head, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could maybe also look during the break. Off the top of my head, I cannot think of any. The only map that I remember was related to another location, not to Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Mladic again would like to consult with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, as you know, you are always invited to remain seated when you consult with counsel. Would you please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't receive any English translation. One second. One second. I don't receive any English translation. Is there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear the English now. Mr. Ivetic, if there's anything Mr. Mladic would like to bring to the attention of the Court, you may do so on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No. No loud speaking. Apparently consultation is over. Mr. Ivetic, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would like to add what the General has just reminded me of, that his own home was in Pofalici and prior to this time-period, the ABiH forces had engaged the local Serb civilians and had -- had engaged in combat against them and had forced them out and that his own home had been under fire and was burning and was seen burning by him in this area precisely, Pofalici, so there was a presence of an enemy force known to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is to be found anywhere in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Mladic is not expected to give testimony in his own case unless he presents himself as a witness and then be cross-examined on whatever he says. So, therefore, in that respect we'll ignore that as a piece of information. And you know how to have this information to be introduced into the proceedings. Mr. Mladic wants to consult again. I suggest that he consults with you during the break. We take the break, and if there's anything to be brought to our attention, we'll give you an opportunity to do so immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome I'm just wondering but I'm also addressing you, Mr. Ivetic, whether we should take a break of 20 minutes or whether you would prefer to have the advantage of a little bit more time - not the same as between yesterday 2.30 and this morning, the time Mr. Ivetic had available - but at least perhaps half an hour before we resume --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be appreciated, Your Honours. And I think our submissions would be less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than an hour, and half an hour would be enough for a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will take a break and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to make further submissions, Mr. Ivetic, P501 was, I think, a question I had put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. And the correct number is P581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P581. That may clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it showed the entirety of the document, which is one page deals with the issue that I was going from memory on. And you also had asked about Pofalici. I was able to find evidence on the record of the matters that the General spoke of, the enemy presence in Pofalici. There's transcript page 15544, dealing precisely with May 1992, Prosecution Witness Robert Donia confirming that the Muslim forces had engaged in combat and against the Serbs -- civilians in Pofalici, and then we have transcript page 8172 which is from time-period of 1994 talking about the UN confirming that the BiH side was shooting from Pofalici. Those were the only two references I could find in the transcript during the break. And I thank you for the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything more specific? Because I read in the transcript of the intercepted conversation, again, if authentic, that there are references made to shoot there, around Dobrovoljacka, up there around Humska and Djure Djakovica Street, up there, which is not a very specific -- at least it sounds as if it is not referring to a very specific target to be engaged. If you could, not necessarily now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can. I did read these. With respect to these two transcript references, the one from 1994 only said it was near the Serbian church in Pofalici which I don't know where that would be located. Dr. Donia's testimony was of a particular time-period but a very general nature not giving any geographic assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties could agree on where those streets were at the time so that it may be close to the church or not close to a church. It may be that it is a very small street, 50 metres, which makes it far more specific or whether it's a very long street, as you find sometimes, then that might assist the Chamber in better understanding your explanation, Mr. Ivetic. If the parties could try to reach an agreement on that, it would be appreciated. Then we move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would also like to put on the record that there apparently was some problem with the interpretation and some problem with microphones which apparently caused Mr. Mladic to be concerned about that, and then -- so the Chamber understands that he intervened at that moment and has -- fully understands that this was the case. Mr. Groome, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just with respect to that -- the Pofalici matter, I would also recall for the Chamber that they received evidence in RM511 about how targeting decision were made. The Chamber will recall a full-size military map that was actually presented in court and the Chamber took some time to review that and of the targets. Your Honour, the first matter I would like to deal with are the characterisations by Mr. Ivetic of the Prosecution's argument. He has made a number of submissions related to this. For example, he said today: "Further, at transcript page 20803, the Prosecution boldly asserts that the taking of UN personnel which the Defence did not raise in our 98 bis submissions is indicative of the common purpose behind the JCE constituting genocidal intent." He also brought to your attention transcript page 20805. He characterised what was there, suggesting a particular interpretation of our submissions related to the six strategic objectives. I have re-read those two pages and believe that our position is clear. I think I articulated our case clearly, and rather than repeat myself now, I would simply ask the Chamber to not -- if it needs to be reminded of my arguments, simply look at those arguments rather than relying solely on Mr. Ivetic's interpretation of them. Mr. Ivetic then addressed the 16th Assembly Session. And my submission with respect to that would be the following: Mladic's long and somewhat meandering speech at the 16th Assembly Session deals with many different topics. To dissect and make submissions about the context of Mladic's comments and submission about how the Chamber should interpret his words is something that is beyond the time that we have today. We have made some submissions placing some things that he said in context. We will deal in detail with this speech in our final trial brief and final submissions. We believe that at this stage of the proceedings the Chamber is able to read Mladic's speech which occurs at a very significant time just before he is appointed the commander of the Main Staff, and the Chamber will be able to come to its own views regarding what inferences are to be drawn from it for the purpose of the decision that the Chamber must take at this juncture in the trial. With respect to perpetrators that were not VRS members, at several points Mr. Ivetic against raised arguments about perpetrators associated with police forces at some points mixing his arguments about those forces with arguments about paramilitaries. The only evidence Mr. Ivetic referred to is evidence from after the majority of mass executions in Srebrenica had been completed, evidence related to Trnopolje or documentary evidence from September or October 1995. Mr. Ivetic presents this evidence as if it relates to crimes by RS police forces in 1992. Instead each document comes after the incidents charged in the indictment in which police forces were involved in committing crimes in partnership with the VRS. In some cases, for instance, related to crimes in detention facilities like Keraterm and Omarska these documents come several years afterwards. Moreover, taken in their entirety, these documents reflect that the JCE members were continuing to use paramilitary forces which they had known for years were committing crimes. Mr. Ivetic also suggested today that the Prosecution did not address certain incidents where he suggested paramilitaries or MUP personnel had been perpetrators. In fact, the Prosecution addressed every Schedule A incident Mr. Ivetic discussed and on Monday, and explained in detail the partnership between different JCE forces in maintaining the system of detention facilities and committing crimes there. With respect to his submissions regarding RM070, the Defence suggests that the use of RM070's testimony and sexual violence related to offences that Mladic was unaware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: However, we turn to the Mladic notebook entries. If the Court considers P357 at page 67, you will see a 14th of January, 1993 meeting of Mladic with Slobodan Milosevic who gives Mladic a list of Muslims to be released from detention. Mladic notes that one of the women is: "She is in Elez prison in Miljevnina." We also ask the Chamber to review Mladic's notebook from November 1993 at P359, page 13, where he specifically notes by name women being held. For additional context, we ask the Trial Chamber to review the closed session testimony of RM048. General Mladic was well aware that women were being held and he did nothing to stop systematic sexual violence inflicted on them. It is also worth noting that P338, page 45, the Main Staff combat readiness report of 1993, explicitly refers to allegations of rapes and various other crimes as part of a "brutal and ruthless anti-Serbian media campaign." So these claims of crimes of sexual violence were dismissed as propaganda, as it were. With respect to submissions regarding Ewa Tabeau, we can say that if the Chamber reviews Ms. Tabeau's report in whole, you will see that the Defence misconstrues the evidence. With respect to the issue of the relevance of events that occurred prior to 12th May, my submissions are rather brief. I think one only has to consider a simple criminal case, such as a murder case, to appreciate that there may very well be relevant evidence of mens rea and planning that occurs before the actual homicide. There's nothing new or controversial about this. The Mladic Defence raised this in a number of objections to the admission of evidence. The Chamber heard and considered the Defence arguments fully. The evidence was admitted and it should not be re-argued now. I won't repeat the rationale for why evidence before an indictment period may be relevant to the indictment period. I believe is self-evident. The differences between Karadzic and Mladic. Mr. Ivetic raises the argument that the relationship between Karadzic and Mladic was such that a JCE could not have existed and points to the issue of Arkan's presence in Sanski Most. It would require a very long time to give a useful narrative about the relationship between the two men over the years. I would simply say that it is important to consider the time and context when examining evidence about their relationship. For example, the situation Mr. Ivetic referred to occurred in 1995 and -- and to understand that, the Chamber really has to understand the context of their relationship at that stage. All I will say in response to Mr. Ivetic's submission is that the professional relationship between Karadzic and Mladic always functioned and functioned well. At no time during the indictment period did tensions between Karadzic and Mladic rise to a level that they compromised their respective participation in or contributions to a common criminal plan or rise to a level which compromised the superior/subordinate relationship between Karadzic and Mladic and Mladic and his subordinates. And I would recall for the -- the Chamber the evidence of General Milovanovic who addressed this -- this very point. During the course of the indictment period, there was from time to time disagreement among JCE members regarding the best way to achieve its goals, but there is ample evidence before the Chamber establishing that the goals remained constant throughout the indictment period. Mr. McCloskey will now address the Chamber on a few matters related to Srebrenica. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. I won't take much of your time today. Mr. Ivetic spoke briefly of Directive 7, and the arguments are -- are out. I won't say anything on that except to reiterate -- and I know you will take a good look at the documents. They speak for themselves. And they stand together, 7 and 7.1. Radovan Karadzic and General Mladic. Consistent with each other. As President Karadzic and General Mladic stood together, as just referenced by Mr. Groome. Mr. Ivetic's allegation regarding the contradiction in the Prosecution's opening statement, I -- from the -- the observations, the questions of the President, I think it cleared that up. The Prosecution has always argued that there was a two-part purpose to the attack on the enclave. One, legitimate; and one illegitimate. And the various arguments and documents based on that remain the same and untouched by Mr. Ivetic's arguments. Mr. Ivetic brought up the testimony of RM374, again, Kravica, and I will very briefly bring out some of the key points there. RM374 met with Colonel Beara in Zvornik. You may -- you will recall that testimony. He also recalled receiving a story from a bus driver who said he was at the Kravica warehouse when a Muslim grabbed a gun from a Serb, and Muslims and Serbs were shot. Now, this version sounds a lot like what we refer to as burned hands, and possibly could be. As you know, the Prosecution does believe that a burned-hands incident happened. That a Muslim at the warehouse came out, grabbed a gun from a Serb policeman, and shot and killed one Serb and wounded another and that people were killed on both sides. There are two interpretations related to the Kravica warehouse. One, that this is what started the incident that led to the murder of some 800 to a thousand men; the burned-hands incident started it. The other version is that it started before that and, as a result of the executions, a Muslim came out, grabbed a gun, and killed a Serb. The first version, the Prosecution feels, is unreasonable. The second version, reasonable. Should the Court differ and find that the first version -- or that both versions are reasonable, we understand the law requires you to take the Defence version. And if you do that, also recall that these men that -- that died at the Kravica warehouse on the evening of 13 July were already marked for death and were killed during the process of the murder operation. But when you're making this important determination about which is reasonable, please recall the testimony of RM256. And if I could bring up one picture from P1539, page 60, that's the road book that was the subject of testimony of Mr. Blaszczyk. And in that book, we see a picture of the Kravica warehouse with bodies in front of it. You'll remember the famous video where Petrovic and Borovcanin are driving by from right to left, and we see bodies in front of the warehouse, camouflaged men with their back to the warehouse, and a bus, and then we hear automatic gun-fire, and then the -- the film goes blank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, since we have some problems with our screens, could you take us to the relevant page so that we could look at it on our own private scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did it -- did it just come up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not for me, but that's already half an hour. So that's -- if you give me the page I'll have a look at it because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 60 of P1539.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is -- it would not have been my first choice because unfortunately this -- these two photos are reversed from the way it was in actuality. If -- if you remember the film as it goes from right to left, the bus is actually on the left side of the bodies, but this separate photograph has been put on the right side of the -- the bodies in -- in the book. So just concentrate on the photo with the bodies and -- and recall that that bus is there but it's on the left side. This is what is the west side of the warehouse, the one with the bodies in front of it. And this is where RM256 is located, not far from that opening. And he is jammed in there with other men, and it's practically full, if not completely full, according to his testimony. And the other side, the east side of the warehouse, according to the testimony, is already full, and that is where the other survivor, RM274, is. And the testimony of RM256 is that a man comes -- a Muslim man is brought into the warehouse, it's so packed he has nowhere to sit, he complains, and then suddenly gun-fire opens up all around them and people are being shot inside the warehouse. Then hand grenades are thrown in, and he manages to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, at the same time, RM274 is in the east side of the warehouse, and his -- his statements say that he hears gun-fire outside that's going on for a while. The most reasonable interpretation of this evidence is that the mass executions begin as they were seen by RM256. This person comes into the warehouse, it's jammed, gun-fire opens up. After that, burned hands happens. If it's the bus, people outside of the bus. It's in reaction to people on the bus hearing and seeing what's going on in the warehouse. Because RM256, if he is just inside this warehouse, he would have heard a burned hands gun-fire that happens outside the warehouse. He would have heard that. Automatic weapon fire you can even hear it on the -- you can hear some automatic weapon fire even on this -- on this video, as -- -- as it drives by. This is an amazing noise. Would have been heard had burned hands happened before that. Also there's evidence of a special police soldier that is ordered by Borovcanin to stop the traffic at the Kravica village. He does so. Shortly after stopping the traffic he hears automatic weapon fire and hand grenades. So it's a complicated situation with many witnesses. Two versions: One reasonable and one unreasonable. And thank you for your -- for your careful attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Groome, does this conclude the submissions by the Prosecution or is there anything you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes, then, this hearing in which the Chamber heard any submissions which would be able to assist us in determining whether Rule 98 bis applies or not. The Chamber will consider the submissions and will -- since specific submissions have been made, will deliver a decision anyhow, which will be an oral decision. I think we have not yet decided when it will be delivered. Therefore, we adjourn for the day but sine die. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.30 a.m.,
